title: A call in secret
hookLine: Zakariyya's bones are weak and hair white, but he's never been disappointed in prayer (19:3–4)

lines: IT OPENS WITH AN OLD MAN.
cards: Surah nineteen is named for a woman: Maryam, the mother of 'Isa, the only woman the Qur'an names. But it doesn't open with her. It opens with an old man, alone, at night, praying so quietly that nobody else could hear.
He's been asking for the same thing for years. Today: his prayer, and the sentence in it that has kept people asking ever since.

teach.b: The old man is Zakariyya, Zechariah, a guardian of the temple and of the young Maryam. In Pickthall's words, the surah calls this a mention of God's mercy to His servant, "When he cried unto his Lord a cry in secret".
Nida'an khafiyya: a hidden call. Why hidden? Commentators suggest humility, or the late hour, or that he was embarrassed to ask, at his age, for a child.

Then he describes himself honestly: my bones have grown weak, and my head is ablaze with white hair. And then, in Pickthall's words: "and I have never been unblest in prayer to Thee, my Lord." Look at the logic.

He doesn't say: I've always gotten what I asked for. He says: I've never come away from asking You empty. His case for asking again isn't his strength, which is gone, or his wife's, who has never had a child.

teach.h: HIS CASE: HIS HISTORY WITH GOD.
teach.b: It's his history with God. Asking has always been good for him, so he asks. He asks for an heir, to carry on the family of Ya'qub.
The answer comes: a son, named Yahya, a name, the surah says, given to no one before him.

teach.h: A SON, AND THREE NIGHTS OF SILENCE.
teach.b: When Zakariyya asks for a sign, he's told he won't speak to people for three nights, though nothing is wrong with him. A man who prayed in secret is given silence.

teach.h: I HAVE NEVER BEEN UNBLEST IN PRAYER TO THEE.
teach.b: A hadith in Muslim's collection sits beside this: a person's prayer is answered as long as they don't grow impatient and say, I prayed and prayed and saw nothing, and give up.

how: Many Muslims make private du'a, often at night, for long-held wishes such as children, and cite Zakariyya's prayer in 19:3–6 and 21:89 as a model of quiet persistence.

o: a loud cry for help in the temple
a vow of silence for three nights
a hidden call, a prayer made in secret

games.q: inside the prayer — tap the pairs.
p: a name given to no one before

s: Surah Maryam opens with Maryam's story
it opens with Zakariyya's prayer; Maryam's story follows.
Zakariyya says he always got what he asked for
he says he was never left wretched or empty in his prayer to God.
a hadith says prayer is answered unless you grow impatient and give up

games.q: you're old, your wife has never had a child, and you've asked for years. what's your case for asking again?
o: your history: asking God has never left you empty.
a promise you were once given.
games.why: Zakariyya admits his weakness, then rests everything on his history with God: never unblest in prayer (19:4).

practice: Think of an old wish, something you asked for once and stopped asking for because nothing seemed to happen, and let it come back without embarrassment.

If you pray, you can ask for it again, quietly, the way Zakariyya did, beginning with honesty about where you are. If you don't, just hold the wish and notice whether you'd given up on it, and whether you want to.

wordCard.voice: Nida'an khafiyya. Zakariyya's hidden call at night, old and honest, built on one fact: asking had never left him empty.

orig.note: Arabic: a hidden call, a secret cry (19:3).

carryVoice: Your line: never disappointed in asking. His case was his history with God. See you tomorrow.
